comparison.summary: Same postorder tree traversal; your solution copies ancestor maps instead of restoring per-letter stacks.
details: Both traverse the original tree, find the nearest ancestor with the same character, and add the completed subtree size to that ancestor or the original parent.
Your DFS computes newParent before setting last for the current node, then passes new Map(last) to each child. It does not need to undo changes on return.
The existing Python and TypeScript maintain a stack of ancestors for each character, push before visiting children, use the previous stack entry as the new parent, and pop on return.
Both take O(n) time and O(n) space with the fixed 26-letter alphabet. The map-copy version has larger constant overhead. No JavaScript implementation was saved.

solutions.title: Recursive DFS with copied ancestor maps
solutions.approach: Traverse the original tree while remembering the closest ancestor for each letter. Give each child its own copy of that map so visiting one child does not change the ancestors seen by another. After finishing a node’s children, add its completed subtree size to the closest same-letter ancestor, or to its original parent if none exists.

variables.n: Number of nodes in the tree.

notes: This is the selected recursive version. A path-shaped tree with 100,000 nodes can exceed JavaScript’s recursion limit; use an iterative version if the runtime rejects deep recursion.
solutions.walkthroughMarkdown:
#### 1. Initialize the original tree

Use `parent = [-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1]` and `s = "abaabc"`. Set `n = 6`, `kids = [[], [], [], [], [], []]`, and `size = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]`. Each node initially counts itself. Letters by node are `0:a`, `1:b`, `2:a`, `3:a`, `4:b`, and `5:c`.

#### 2. Build every child list

Initialize the construction loop with `node = 1`; node `0` is the root and has no parent.

At `node = 1`, `1 < 6` is true. Read `parent[1] = 0` and execute `kids[0].push(1)`. Now `kids = [[1], [], [], [], [], []]`. Increase `node` to `2`.

At `node = 2`, `2 < 6` is true. Read `parent[2] = 0` and execute `kids[0].push(2)`. Now `kids = [[1, 2], [], [], [], [], []]`. Increase `node` to `3`.

At `node = 3`, `3 < 6` is true. Read `parent[3] = 1` and execute `kids[1].push(3)`. Now `kids = [[1, 2], [3], [], [], [], []]`. Increase `node` to `4`.

At `node = 4`, `4 < 6` is true. Read `parent[4] = 1` and execute `kids[1].push(4)`. Now `kids = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [], [], [], []]`. Increase `node` to `5`.

At `node = 5`, `5 < 6` is true. Read `parent[5] = 1` and execute `kids[1].push(5)`. Now `kids = [[1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [], [], [], []]`. Increase `node` to `6`.

At `node = 6`, `6 < 6` is false. Finish building `kids`. These lists describe the original tree and are not rewritten during DFS.

#### 3. Traverse the original tree and accumulate modified subtree sizes

Call `dfs(0, new Map())`. In each entry below, `last` maps a letter to the nearest ancestor carrying that letter. Each child receives a separate copy.

**Enter `dfs(0, {})`.** Read `char = s[0] = "a"` and initialize `newParent = parent[0] = -1`.

Check `last.has("a")`: `false`.

Keep the original `newParent = -1` because no ancestor has this letter.

Execute `last.set("a", 0)`. This call’s Map becomes `{"a": 0}`. Its child list is `kids[0] = [1, 2]`.

For child `1`, create `new Map(last) = {"a": 0}` and call `dfs(1, that copy)`. The parent call’s Map remains separate.

**Enter `dfs(1, {"a": 0})`.** Read `char = s[1] = "b"` and initialize `newParent = parent[1] = 0`.

Check `last.has("b")`: `false`.

Keep the original `newParent = 0` because no ancestor has this letter.

Execute `last.set("b", 1)`. This call’s Map becomes `{"a": 0, "b": 1}`. Its child list is `kids[1] = [3, 4, 5]`.

For child `3`, create `new Map(last) = {"a": 0, "b": 1}` and call `dfs(3, that copy)`. The parent call’s Map remains separate.

**Enter `dfs(3, {"a": 0, "b": 1})`.** Read `char = s[3] = "a"` and initialize `newParent = parent[3] = 1`.

Check `last.has("a")`: `true`.

Read `last.get("a") = 0` and assign `newParent = 0`. This is the nearest matching ancestor on the original path.

Execute `last.set("a", 3)`. This call’s Map becomes `{"a": 3, "b": 1}`. Its child list is `kids[3] = []`.

There are no children to visit. Check `newParent !== -1`: `0 !== -1` is `true`.

Execute `size[0] += size[3]`: `1 + 1 = 2`. The complete size array becomes `[2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

Reach the end of `dfs(3, last)` and return to its caller.

**Resume node `1` after child `3`.** This call still has `last = {"a": 0, "b": 1}`; child changes did not alter it. Current sizes are `[2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

For child `4`, create `new Map(last) = {"a": 0, "b": 1}` and call `dfs(4, that copy)`. The parent call’s Map remains separate.

**Enter `dfs(4, {"a": 0, "b": 1})`.** Read `char = s[4] = "b"` and initialize `newParent = parent[4] = 1`.

Check `last.has("b")`: `true`.

Read `last.get("b") = 1` and assign `newParent = 1`. This is the nearest matching ancestor on the original path.

Execute `last.set("b", 4)`. This call’s Map becomes `{"a": 0, "b": 4}`. Its child list is `kids[4] = []`.

There are no children to visit. Check `newParent !== -1`: `1 !== -1` is `true`.

Execute `size[1] += size[4]`: `1 + 1 = 2`. The complete size array becomes `[2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

Reach the end of `dfs(4, last)` and return to its caller.

**Resume node `1` after child `4`.** This call still has `last = {"a": 0, "b": 1}`; child changes did not alter it. Current sizes are `[2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

For child `5`, create `new Map(last) = {"a": 0, "b": 1}` and call `dfs(5, that copy)`. The parent call’s Map remains separate.

**Enter `dfs(5, {"a": 0, "b": 1})`.** Read `char = s[5] = "c"` and initialize `newParent = parent[5] = 1`.

Check `last.has("c")`: `false`.

Keep the original `newParent = 1` because no ancestor has this letter.

Execute `last.set("c", 5)`. This call’s Map becomes `{"a": 0, "b": 1, "c": 5}`. Its child list is `kids[5] = []`.

There are no children to visit. Check `newParent !== -1`: `1 !== -1` is `true`.

Execute `size[1] += size[5]`: `2 + 1 = 3`. The complete size array becomes `[2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

Reach the end of `dfs(5, last)` and return to its caller.

**Resume node `1` after child `5`.** This call still has `last = {"a": 0, "b": 1}`; child changes did not alter it. Current sizes are `[2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

All children `[3, 4, 5]` have returned. Check `newParent !== -1`: `0 !== -1` is `true`.

Execute `size[0] += size[1]`: `2 + 3 = 5`. The complete size array becomes `[5, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

Reach the end of `dfs(1, last)` and return to its caller.

**Resume node `0` after child `1`.** This call still has `last = {"a": 0}`; child changes did not alter it. Current sizes are `[5, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

For child `2`, create `new Map(last) = {"a": 0}` and call `dfs(2, that copy)`. The parent call’s Map remains separate.

**Enter `dfs(2, {"a": 0})`.** Read `char = s[2] = "a"` and initialize `newParent = parent[2] = 0`.

Check `last.has("a")`: `true`.

Read `last.get("a") = 0` and assign `newParent = 0`. This is the nearest matching ancestor on the original path.

Execute `last.set("a", 2)`. This call’s Map becomes `{"a": 2}`. Its child list is `kids[2] = []`.

There are no children to visit. Check `newParent !== -1`: `0 !== -1` is `true`.

Execute `size[0] += size[2]`: `5 + 1 = 6`. The complete size array becomes `[6, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

Reach the end of `dfs(2, last)` and return to its caller.

**Resume node `0` after child `2`.** This call still has `last = {"a": 0}`; child changes did not alter it. Current sizes are `[6, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`.

All children `[1, 2]` have returned. Check `newParent !== -1`: `-1 !== -1` is `false`.

The root has no parent, so there is no size addition.

Reach the end of `dfs(0, last)` and return to `findSubtreeSizes`.

#### 4. Return the completed sizes

Return `size = [6, 3, 1, 1, 1, 1]`. Node `3` moves from original parent `1` to matching ancestor `0`; node `1` keeps only itself and nodes `4` and `5`, giving size `3`. Root `0` still contains all six nodes.

Sizes are added after child calls return. A moved child contributes directly to its new parent, while the recursive traversal still follows the original `kids` lists.

With `n` nodes and a fixed 26-letter alphabet, each copied Map has at most 26 entries. Time is `O(n)` and total extra space is `O(n)` for child lists, sizes, copied Maps, and recursion.
